research.approach: Fitness practitioners treat membership as a leaky bucket: with about 45 members leaving for every 40 joining, they fix the leak and the tap together, leak first because it is cheaper. They measure retention by months of membership and join source, find out why people leave with a short exit survey plus conversations and with behaviour signals such as falling attendance, then run a first-90-days routine (welcome in 24 hours, a habit window, a check-in near day 60), and act early on members whose own attendance pattern slips, offering freezes or downgrades rather than discounts. For new members they run a small, local test with a low-friction trial offer, a page or form built for the ad, fast follow-up, and a funnel read from lead to trial to member, not cost per lead. Ads must avoid language that implies something about the viewer's body.

sources.title: Why are members cancelling my gym? (Keepme)
sources.note: Vendor blog. Reasons are blunt in forms, so pair exit surveys with conversations; watch attendance drops and freeze or cancellation-page visits; measure retention by tenure, cohort and lead source; offer controlled alternatives such as freezes.

sources.title: How to reduce gym member churn: a practical retention system (FitHive)
sources.note: Vendor blog. Judge each member against their own pattern, sort into risk levels with a named owner and response, diagnose before offering anything, track cohort retention at 90, 180 and 365 days; pitfalls include discounting instead of diagnosing and generic messages.

sources.title: How to retain new gym members: the 90-day retention strategy (Clubworx)
sources.note: Vendor blog, figures unsourced. Welcome within 24 hours, track attendance in days 8 to 42, personal check-in around day 60.

sources.title: Fitness Facebook ads statistics 2026: CPC, CPL and conversion benchmarks (Webtonic)
sources.note: Agency blog, benchmarks directional. Track cost per trial booking, show-up rate, trial-to-member rate; send paid traffic to a page built for it; tight radius; avoid asking for a card up front; watch saturation.

sources.title: 2026 health advertising policies on social media (Accelerated Digital Media)
sources.note: Agency summary, not Meta's own page: ads may not assert or imply a viewer's personal attributes or put down appearance; verify against Meta's current policy pages before launch.

steps.name: Write down the promises and ad rules first
steps.why: The gym's no-lock-in promise and the Meta rules on body-related wording shape every offer, message and ad, so they are fixed before anything is written.

steps.name: Measure the member flow and check the counts
steps.why: Active members, joins, cancellations and freezes by month, and months of membership at cancellation, show whether the leak is early or late. The reported 610, 45 and 40 are checked against the export and definitions first.

steps.name: Find out why members leave
steps.why: The reason has never been asked. Practitioners combine a short exit survey with a follow-up conversation and the behaviour signals before the cancellation, since stated reasons such as price are blunt.

steps.name: Build a first-90-days routine
steps.why: Early weeks decide who forms a habit. Practitioners send a welcome within a day, check the first sessions, watch attendance in the habit window and hold a progress check-in near day 60.

steps.name: Act early on members whose attendance is slipping
steps.why: Cancellations build over weeks. Each member is judged against their own pattern, sorted into risk levels with a named owner, and offered the fix that matches the problem, such as a schedule change, freeze or downgrade, not a blanket discount.

steps.name: Run a small local trial-offer test
steps.why: To add members, practitioners test a low-friction trial or first-month offer to people near the gym, with a landing page or lead form built for it, a tight radius, copy that follows Meta's rules, and spend capped to the budget.

steps.name: Follow up fast and read the whole funnel
steps.why: Cost per lead is not the result. Practitioners count leads, trial bookings, trials attended, members joined and cost per member, and respond quickly to each lead.

steps.name: Read members monthly by cohort and source
steps.why: Active members are tracked monthly with retention by join month and source, so the effect of each change is read separately and the path to 750 stays honest.

pitfalls.text: Discounting or sending generic we-miss-you messages instead of diagnosing why a member is drifting.
Treating the exit-form reason, especially price, as the whole story.
Judging ads by cost per lead, or sending paid traffic to a homepage.
Ad wording that implies something about the viewer's body, which Meta can reject.
Relying on one blended retention number that hides which members and which months leak.

hypotheses.statement: Most cancellations come from members in their first three months.
hypotheses.test: Cancellations by months of membership at the time of leaving, for the last 12 months.
hypotheses.confirm_if: A large share of cancellations has under three months of membership.
hypotheses.refute_if: Cancellations are spread across long-standing members.

hypotheses.statement: Members visibly drift before they cancel, so many cancellations could be caught early.
hypotheses.test: Compare each cancelled member's visits in the 8 weeks before cancelling with their earlier pattern.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Most cancelled members show a clear fall in visits well before cancelling.
hypotheses.refute_if: Many cancel with steady attendance and no earlier signal.

hypotheses.statement: Certain classes, times or crowded sessions drive members away.
hypotheses.test: Retention and cancellations by main class type, time slot and class fill rate where available.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Members of certain classes or crowded slots leave at clearly higher rates.
hypotheses.refute_if: Retention is similar across classes and times.

hypotheses.statement: A large share of cancellations is unavoidable, such as moves, injury or season, so retention cannot carry the target alone.
hypotheses.test: Exit survey reasons grouped as preventable or not, and cancellations by month.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Most stated reasons are life changes, or cancellations bunch in particular seasons.
hypotheses.refute_if: Most reasons are about value, schedule, crowding or service.

hypotheses.statement: Members who joined from some sources or intro offers leave much faster.
hypotheses.test: Retention at 90 days by join source and intro offer, with volume noted.
hypotheses.confirm_if: One source or offer with enough volume has clearly worse retention.

hypotheses.statement: Interested people are lost because trial requests are answered slowly or not tracked.
hypotheses.test: Weekly funnel tally of leads, time to first reply, trials booked and attended, and joins.
hypotheses.confirm_if: Many leads are contacted late or never, and trials booked rarely turn into joins.
hypotheses.refute_if: Leads are answered quickly and the drop is elsewhere.

hypotheses.statement: Meta ads have not been tested with a local trial offer, so there is untapped demand within a short distance.
hypotheses.test: Read past Meta results for any local trial offer; judge demand from the capped test, not from estimates.
hypotheses.confirm_if: The test brings trial bookings that attend and join at a cost per member the owners accept.
hypotheses.refute_if: Past or test results show leads that do not book or join.

measurement.window: Monthly until June 1; each retention routine is read after at least one full 90-day cohort, each ad test after the lead and trial counts agreed before launch.
measurement.min_volume: Read retention for groups only with the member counts the owners agree before the first read; ad tests need the lead and trial counts agreed before launch.
measurement.stop_rule: Pause any message or ad that breaks the no-lock-in promise or draws complaints; stop ad spend that would pass 2,000 dollars in a month.
